title: Live-In Guardians for Probate Houses
one_liner: Vetted live-in 'guardians' keep a house occupied while an estate is in probate, so the executor keeps insurance validity, avoids vacancy losses and pays less than for a vacant-home policy.
customer: Executors, estate and probate attorneys, professional fiduciaries and out-of-state heirs holding an inherited house. Attorneys are the channel, and executors and estates pay.
problem: Probate sales often take 6 to 12 months or longer. Most homeowners policies limit or exclude coverage after 30 to 60 days of vacancy, so a burst pipe, vandal or squatter can leave the estate uncovered, and specialty vacant-home policies cost far more. The executor is a non-expert with fiduciary liability, often living out of state, and has no one to check the house.
solution: Place screened guardians (night-shift nurses, travel clinicians, grad students, apprentice tradespeople) in probate houses under a state-specific license agreement rather than a lease. Guardians pay a low monthly fee, keep utilities on, handle mail and lawn, and file daily check-in logs. The estate gets an 'occupied' attestation accepted by a partner insurer or MGA, monthly photo reports, and a house that shows better at sale time. Upsell cleanout and staging at sale.
why_now: Boomer estates are moving through probate in growing numbers, and homeowners insurers are tightening on nonrenewals and vacancy. Housing costs are high enough that many good tenants will accept a small duty load for below-market housing. UK-style property guardianship exists for commercial buildings, but the US probate house niche is open.
revenue_model: Estate pays $250 to $500 per month service fee. Guardian pays a program fee. Carrier or MGA commission on the policy. Fees on cleanout, staging and sale-transition services.
non_obvious_insight: The customer isn't buying a house sitter; the estate is buying continued insurance validity and a checklist that satisfies a fiduciary. Occupied status changes the risk class of the asset for the whole probate period. Legal structure (license, not lease, chosen state by state) is the real product and the barrier to copycats.
first_30_days: Pitch 15 probate and estate-planning attorneys in one metro on a pilot for their next three vacant homes. Recruit guardians through hospital and travel-nurse groups. Have a landlord-tenant attorney draft the license and pick a landlord-friendly state to start (for example Texas or Tennessee). Line up a vacant-dwelling insurance broker who will recognize the guardian arrangement. First revenue within about six weeks.

title: Hospital Back-Office Campuses Become Staff Housing
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Real estate (office-to-resi, vacancy, property mgmt, affordability)
one_liner: Help nonprofit health systems convert surplus administrative office campuses, emptied by AI scribes and revenue-cycle automation, into staff housing, with the hospital itself as the master-lease credit that makes the conversion financeable.
customer: Nonprofit health-system CFOs and real-estate heads pay a fixed-fee feasibility engagement plus a success fee. Development and lending partners are secondary.
problem: Health systems own large billing, coding and admin campuses just as ambient AI (over 70% of large delivery networks have deployed or piloted scribes) and revenue-cycle automation shrink back-office headcount. Medicaid work requirements threaten 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hits, and replacing a bedside nurse costs roughly $55-60K by industry surveys. Meanwhile office-conversion lenders will not fund without a credit tenant, and 2026 rates are punishing.
solution: A 'space-to-housing' package: a utilization audit of admin real estate (badge, Wi-Fi and parking data), floor-by-floor conversion screening, a 10-15 year staff-housing master lease structured as a recruiting and retention benefit (rent by payroll deduction), tax-exempt or community-benefit financing, and a co-development partner. Fee at financial close.
why_now: AI scribes and RCM automation went mainstream in 2025-26, and Medicaid cuts force hospitals to monetize idle assets. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months. Public-partnered conversions such as 100 Gold Street (4,000 units) show a mission-aligned pipeline. PE physician-practice deals are down about 50%, so systems are holding more real estate.
revenue_model: $40-90K feasibility fee, a 1-2% success fee or development-fee share at close, ongoing asset-management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in office conversion is not design but a credit tenant. A hospital is the rare mission-aligned credit with a hard-dollar reason to want housing (turnover cost), and its own back offices are the least visible vacancy on the market.
first_30_days: Build a public-data list of 30 nonprofit systems with admin campuses (IRS Schedule H, county records, satellite parking counts). Cold-pitch a free two-page 'vacancy read' to their real-estate VPs. Convert 2-3 into paid audits within 90 days.

title: Translator-Owned Language Trusts for Public Services
one_liner: Translator co-ops that build and license verified medical, legal, and benefits corpora for refugee and diaspora languages, and sell certified human review to agencies that now rely on machine translation.
customer: State Medicaid and benefits agencies, hospital systems, courts, and school districts serving speakers of Karen, Somali, Kirundi, Tigrinya, Haitian Creole, Hmong, Dari, and similar languages. Agencies pay per-word review and $50-150k annual contracts. AI labs and voice-AI vendors license evaluation and fine-tuning data.
problem: General translation is commoditized, so translators are displaced. But in low-resource languages, machine translation of consent forms, discharge instructions, and benefits notices is wrong in dangerous ways, and agencies use it because human capacity has evaporated. Translators' glossaries and corrections are given away or locked in agency-owned translation memories, and gig data platforms pay a pittance.
solution: A member-owned trust per language cluster. Translators contribute and verify domain glossaries and parallel corpora under community governance with consent, revenue share, and veto rights. The trust sells (a) certified human review of machine-translated public-service documents with a warranty, (b) benchmarks and licensed data to vendors, with usage royalties passed to members, and (c) an MT-plus-human-guardrails workflow for agencies.
why_now: The HHS Section 1557 rule (2024) requires qualified human review when machine translation is used on critical health documents, and it remains in effect in 2026, which creates non-discretionary demand. The Mozilla Data Collective opened paid commercial licensing of community datasets and the Gates Foundation has committed to language AI. Freelance translation rates have collapsed.
revenue_model: Per-word certified-review fees, annual agency retainers, data and benchmark licenses, and patronage dividends to member translators.
non_obvious_insight: A translator's most valuable asset is not their time but their error corrections in narrow domains, which is precisely what every model is worst at. The co-op structure solves both community trust and individual freelancers' lack of bargaining power, and legal language-access duties turn the buyer's budget from discretionary to mandatory.
first_30_days: Pick one language and one metro with a large diaspora, such as Karen speakers in St. Paul. Recruit 10-15 translators as founding members. Offer a hospital system or county health department a paid pilot to review its top 50 patient documents against Section 1557 requirements. Build the glossary in shared tooling and sign a governance charter.

title: Safe-Deposit Box Successor With Heir Protocol
one_liner: A bonded, insured vault subscription for original wills, deeds, titles, seed-phrase backups and heirlooms, with a scripted release protocol for heirs, sold through estate attorneys as the bank box disappears.
customer: Estate-planning and elder-law attorneys as the channel, and their clients aged 55 to 85 whose plan says 'the original is in the safe deposit box'. Secondary: coin, gold and crypto holders, and small landlords and business owners holding original deeds and titles.
problem: Chase said in August 2025 that it would phase out all remaining safe deposit boxes nationwide, after it stopped new rentals in 2021. Capital One, Santander and Citizens exited earlier, and the total number of boxes has reportedly fallen from about 40M to an estimated 25M to 32M. Contents are not FDIC-insured, and no federal law governs boxes. On a death the bank typically freezes access until paperwork clears. The box was the default chain of custody for the paper that proves who owns what, and nothing has replaced it.
solution: Rent standardized boxes or sealed envelopes inside licensed, bonded vault partners. Each item gets a photo and hash inventory, and contents are insured under a valuables policy. The core product is a designated-heir protocol: on a death certificate plus an attorney letter or executor's letters, the vault releases to the named person after video attestation and dual control. Add periodic proof-of-life check-ins, an index the attorney can see, and an original-will custody service tied to the attorney's office.
why_now: Chase's nationwide phase-out (announced August 2025) removed the largest holder of boxes. The Great Wealth Transfer is under way. Retail gold and crypto holdings create new 'irreplaceable original' items such as seed backups and coins that people do not want in a home closet.
revenue_model: $15 to $35 per month per box, or $199 to $399 per year. A $99 onboarding and inventory fee. A $250 heir-release fee. A white-label or referral share of $5 to $10 per client per month for law firms. Margin on the insurance premium.
non_obvious_insight: The box was never about valuables. It was legal chain of custody for original paper, and banks are quitting because vault space is expensive real estate, not because the need went away. The product is the death protocol that banks never offered, since banks freeze access and a vault plus an attorney workflow can release to the named heir within days. Attorneys are the distribution because they carry malpractice risk when originals are lost.
first_30_days: Check whether your state regulates safe-deposit companies, then sign a white-label deal with one existing bonded vault or secure records-storage operator in a single metro. Draft the release protocol and client agreement with two estate attorneys. Present to 5 estate-planning firms and one senior center with a free 'Where are your originals?' inventory worksheet as the lead magnet. Sell 30 founding-member boxes at a discounted annual rate and run the first two mock heir releases to prove the protocol.

title: Whey Capture Skids for Small Cheesemakers
one_liner: Leased containerized filtration skids that turn small cheese plants' cheap whey into sellable protein concentrate.
customer: Regional and farmstead cheese plants that sell whey for pennies or pay to dispose of it.
problem: Whey protein is scarce and pricey, yet small plants lack the ultrafiltration equipment and offtake to capture it, because equipment makers sell to giants.
solution: A leased, containerized ultrafiltration and diafiltration skid on revenue share, producing liquid whey protein concentrate that we sell to partner dryers and beverage makers.
why_now: Whey concentrate is up 108% in two years and isolate reaches $14/lb, so the byproduct now outearns its economics at small scale.
revenue_model: Skid lease plus a 30-40% revenue share on concentrate sold.
non_obvious_insight: The byproduct ate the product, and the largest untapped upside sits with small plants that big equipment vendors ignore.
first_30_days: Tour five plants in WI, VT and CA, quote a used UF skid, and pre-sell offtake to one beverage brand and one dryer.

title: Pull-the-Plug Testing for Hospitals and Water Plants
one_liner: Bring data center-grade full-facility blackout testing to hospitals, water utilities and other critical facilities that never actually pull the plug, and help them source scarce backup gear the AI build-out has hoarded.
customer: Critical-access and rural hospitals, water and wastewater districts, 911 centers, cold-chain warehouses and municipal facilities. Secondary payers: property insurers, hospital captives and risk pools that can subsidize tests or discount premiums for certified resilience.
problem: Routine emergency-power testing is usually a short, partial-load generator run. It rarely exercises the whole chain (utility loss, ATS transfer, sequenced load pickup, cooling, fuel supply, paralleling controls) under real load, so the interaction failures show up during the actual storm or grid event. At the same time the AI build-out has swallowed generator, switchgear and transformer production, with multi-year lead times, so a failed generator or breaker at a small hospital cannot be replaced quickly. Facility managers know their fragile points but have no credible way to test them or to find spares.
solution: A one-day 'controlled blackout' service using data center IST discipline: written sequence-of-operations script, load-bank top-up to real facility load, thermographic and breaker health checks before and after, a witnessed utility-loss transfer, fuel/cooling/ventilation checks, and a punch list. Deliver a resilience certificate with prioritized fixes and remaining-life estimates. Upsell: source and retest certified pre-owned generators, ATS and switchgear from cancelled or paused data center orders, and keep a small regional spares pool for members of a hospital or water-district cooperative.
why_now: AI infrastructure is consuming electrical gear supply (transformer lead times of 3-5 years, switchgear reportedly sold out into 2028) while nearly half of planned 2026 US data center builds are delayed or canceled, which leaves stranded but scarce gear. Storm and grid-stress events are also raising the stakes for small critical facilities. Insurers are scrutinizing resilience, and rural facilities cannot afford the big-firm engineering studies.
revenue_model: $18K-45K per facility test; annual re-test contracts; 10-15% sourcing margin on certified pre-owned gear; insurer or captive partnership fees per policyholder tested; small monthly membership for spares-pool access.
non_obvious_insight: In a data center nobody trusts backup power until someone has pulled the plug at full load, and most first tests find something. The rest of critical infrastructure, which arguably matters more, almost never does this because the fear of a failed test outweighs the fear of a failed emergency. A Cx lead who has run hundreds of pull-the-plug tests can make the test routine and safe. The AI boom also turns the spare-gear problem into a secondary market that only someone who has seen the cancellations firsthand can source from.
first_30_days: Rent a 500 kW-1 MW load bank and partner with an electrical contractor. Call 10 facility directors at critical-access hospitals and rural water districts through state hospital and rural water associations. Offer 2 discounted first tests in exchange for case studies and insurer introductions. Approach one regional property insurer or hospital captive with a loss-prevention pilot. Start a private list of sellers of surplus gensets and switchgear from paused data center projects.

title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.
customer: Laid-off ops, finance and product managers with severance or savings of about $100-300K, who pay cohort tuition and a success fee. Second customer: retiring owners of scrap and recycling businesses who want a successor buyer. SBA lenders are a channel.
problem: Mid-career job searches now run 7-13 months with near-zero interview rates (HN threads), and the hiring freeze is hitting degree-holders. Meanwhile thousands of owner-run recycling businesses have no successor. Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.
solution: Build a target database from state solid-waste and hazardous-waste permit records, scrap-dealer licenses and owner age. Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing a large pool of capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: In recycling the scarce input is not technology or capital but a competent successor operator, and the labor market is now manufacturing them. Permits are the moat, so the right move is to buy permitted cash flow instead of financing new plants.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states. Run a free webinar for laid-off managers through layoff-tracker and career communities and enroll a first cohort of about 10. Get two retiring owners to sign exclusive sell-side LOIs. Sign an environmental-consulting partner for a flat-fee diligence pack, and one SBA lender as the financing partner.

title: Work-From-Abroad Compliance Ledger for Employers
one_liner: A Slack-native ledger that tracks where remote employees actually work and flags tax, payroll, permanent-establishment and visa thresholds before 30 days from Lisbon becomes a liability.
customer: Remote-first companies with 50-1,000 employees, their HR and finance teams, and the tax advisors who serve them.
problem: Over 40 countries have nomad visas with thresholds from under USD 1,000 to over USD 7,000 per month, and some ban local employment. The EU Entry/Exit System has tracked non-EU travellers' 90/180-day stays automatically since April 2026. Employees informally work abroad, and companies do not know their exposure. Consumer trackers show individuals their days but give employers no aggregate view or approval flow.
solution: An opt-in ledger built from calendar entries, flight emails and optional device location, with a rules engine per country (183-day tests, 90/180 rules, permanent-establishment risk days, social-security thresholds, nomad-visa work rules). Employees request a workation, get an auto-check, then a manager approves. Export an evidence pack for tax advisors.
why_now: EES is fully live since April 2026, nomad visas keep multiplying, tax authorities are tightening, and return-to-office fights push employees to work from abroad informally.
revenue_model: USD 4-8 per employee per month with a USD 2K annual minimum, plus advisor referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the employer holding the liability, not the nomad. Information is free (Nomads.com sells lifetime membership for USD 1), so value has moved to compliance evidence and approval workflow.
first_30_days: Interview 20 HR leads at remote startups through remote-first communities. Build a Slack bot that answers '/workation Lisbon 6/1-6/30' with rules for 10 countries. Charge a flat USD 150 per month and partner with 2 international tax firms.

title: Break-Glass Interim Operators for Deceased Owners' Businesses
angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x Death, estates and the great wealth transfer
one_liner: An on-call bench of laid-off COOs and ops directors who step in within 48 hours when the sole owner of a small business dies, keeping it alive until the heirs can sell or close it.
customer: Estate attorneys, CPAs, SBA lenders and key-person insurers who need the business to keep its value, plus the widow or heirs. The estate ultimately pays from business cash flow or sale proceeds. Target businesses: HVAC and trades firms, machine shops, independent insurance agencies, restaurants and other 5-50 employee owner-dependent companies.
problem: Probate treats assets as inert (houses, accounts), but a running business melts within 90 days when the owner dies: bank signing authority, payroll, licenses, customer relationships and key employees all hinge on one person. Executors are grieving family. Attorneys cannot run a company. Brokers cannot sell one in freefall. Boomers still own a large share of employer businesses, so this is a huge, mostly invisible transfer.
solution: A vetted bench of interim managers with a 72-hour playbook: secure bank and payroll access via letters testamentary or a special administrator, notify customers and vendors, fund key-employee retention from the estate, arrange licensing 'qualifier' coverage where required, stabilize for 60-90 days, prep a data room, then hand off to a broker or buyer. AI tools (contract abstraction, bookkeeping analysis, KPI dashboards) let a newcomer understand the business in about a week. Owners can pre-buy a 'continuity plan' retainer.
why_now: The largest generational transfer of small businesses is under way (Cerulli: $124T through 2048, about 81% from Boomers and older), while the 2026 labor market is full of experienced ops leaders who cannot find roles. Cheap AI document and finance tooling makes fast onboarding of an unfamiliar business feasible for the first time.
revenue_model: Interim GM day rate of $900-1,500 billed to the estate, with the bench member keeping about 65%. Pre-need continuity retainer of about $1,200/yr for solo owners. Success fee on a sale, in coordination with brokers.
non_obvious_insight: The estate needs a verb, not a noun. The legal system has a process for distributing what a person owned but none for continuing what a person did. Unemployed senior operators are the perfect supply for that verb, and their downside is only the awkwardness of arriving during grief.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 laid-off ops and finance leaders. Write the 72-hour playbook. Offer a free 'owner-death readiness check' at bar association and CPA society events for 30 attorneys and accountants. Sell a $1,200/yr continuity retainer to 20 solo-owner businesses through one insurance agency or SBA lender's client list. The first at-need engagements will come from those attorneys' existing clients.

title: Closure-as-a-Service for Colleges and Grad Programs
one_liner: Orchestrating orderly teach-outs, transcript custody and student transfers for shutting colleges and graduate programs that the new loan caps and demographics are about to gut.
customer: Small private colleges and graduate programs facing closure or merger, state higher-ed regulators, accreditors, and university systems absorbing programs.
problem: The enrollment cliff plus the end of Grad PLUS and the new caps push small colleges and grad programs (nursing, counseling and others) below viability. Closures are chaotic: teach-out agreements, records custody, transfer-credit mapping, refunds and student communications are improvised, and regulators and accreditors demand teach-out plans.
solution: A standing playbook, software and partner network: pre-negotiated teach-out partners, an AI-assisted transfer-credit mapper across receiving schools, secure transcript and records custody, student communications, and tracking of closure obligations. Sell a 'teach-out readiness audit' and retainer to at-risk institutions before they need it.
why_now: The July 2026 aid reset, K-12 and college demographic cliffs and rising closures make this a recurring workload. State regulators are searching for standard processes.
revenue_model: $20-50k annual readiness retainers, $100-400k per closure project, $5-15 per student per year records custody, and referral fees from receiving institutions.
non_obvious_insight: Institutions treat closure as a one-time catastrophe, but with hundreds at risk it is a recurring, standardizable service, like a bankruptcy trustee, where fees come from the estate and reputation for orderly process determines who gets hired.
first_30_days: Publish a teach-out readiness checklist. Offer a $7.5k readiness audit to 10 small colleges and 2 state regulators. Recruit an ex-registrar and an ex-accreditation consultant as delivery leads.

title: Consented Elder-Speech Data Co-op via Storytelling Clubs
angle: Pairing 1: Aging & silver economy x Creator economy / AI provenance
one_liner: Senior-living oral-history clubs where residents opt in, get a life-story book and pay, and their de-identified speech is licensed under strict speech-recognition-only, no-cloning terms to voice-AI and ambient-scribe companies.
customer: Speech-AI, ambient clinical documentation, hearing-aid and companion-robot teams buying elder-speech training and test data (per audio hour). Senior-living operators host the clubs for engagement and a revenue share, and families receive the recordings.
problem: Voice and scribe AI is tuned on younger speech and underperforms on 80+ voices, hearing-aid users and dementia, Parkinson's or stroke speech. AI labs now need clean chain-of-title (Suno swapped to a licensed-data model on Sep 9), and older adults are adopting AI (23% of 65+) while distrusting how their data is used (69% of 50+ are uncomfortable sharing health records with AI). The people who could supply ethical data, and who deserve to be paid for it, have no rights infrastructure.
solution: Trained facilitators (retired teachers, social workers) run recorded storytelling sessions in senior-living communities. Every participant passes a capacity screen with a family or health-care-proxy co-signature and can withdraw. Each clip carries a machine-readable consent scope (recognition and understanding only, never voice synthesis or cloning), is de-identified, and is tracked in a rights ledger that supports revocation and audit. Residents receive cash, the community gets a share, and families get an edited memoir and audio archive.
why_now: Licensed-data pressure is peaking after music and text lawsuits, and the EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency rules began applying in Aug 2026. Voice AI is being pushed on seniors just as they adopt it, and the 80+ cohort is the fastest growing group in the country.
revenue_model: Buyers pay roughly $80-150 per audio hour under a per-dataset license. About 25-30% goes to participants, 15% to the host community, and the rest covers facilitators and platform costs. Family memoir and archive packages are a $149-299 upsell.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not more hours of speech. It is consented hours from the oldest speakers, and only eldercare operators can gather them ethically, because capacity screening, proxies and revocation are the whole product. The strictest license terms (recognition only, no cloning) are what let elders and families say yes.
first_30_days: Pilot in 3 communities with an ethics review from a local university IRB or elder-law adviser. Record about 40 hours and secure a letter of intent from 2 to 3 elder-focused voice or scribe teams for a 100-hour dataset. Use the memoir book as the participant-facing hook.

title: Broker Spread Reveal: Two-Sided Freight Ledger
one_liner: Match what shippers paid brokers against what carriers were actually paid, so every broker's true margin by lane becomes visible for the first time.
customer: Mid-market shippers with $20M to $300M in annual freight spend, using 2 to 6 brokers with no real audit, including PE-owned manufacturers and distributors. Secondary buyers are owner-operators and small carriers at $19 to $49 a month, and freight-procurement consultancies.
problem: Each side holds half the ledger. The shipper knows what it paid the broker. The carrier knows what the broker paid it, on the rate confirmation in the glovebox. The broker's spread, commonly 10 to 35%, stays invisible. Freight-audit firms check invoices against contract rates but never see the carrier payout. 49 CFR 371.3 already requires brokers to keep records of shipper rate, carrier rate and margin. The 2024 proposal to require electronic records and a 48-hour response had still not been finalized as of 2026 status reports. Individual drivers who ask for the record get ghosted.
solution: Carriers text or email a photo of each rate confirmation to a bot. Claude vision extracts lane, dates, load number, broker and pay. Shippers upload freight invoices or a TMS export. The engine pairs the two by load number, origin and destination, and date, then produces a shipper dashboard: 'You paid $412K, carriers received $331K, effective broker take 19.6%. Broker A averages 12% on Chicago to Atlanta, Broker B 27%.' It also generates ready-to-send 371.3 record requests. Aggregated, anonymized carrier-side data becomes a 'Broker Take Index' by lane, giving shippers a benchmark for re-bidding and giving carriers a list of which brokers keep the most.
why_now: The pending 2024 rulemaking has put broker margin disclosure on every carrier's and shipper's radar. The Montgomery ruling has brokers on the defensive. Soft freight markets in 2025 to 2026 have shippers squeezing logistics spend. Vision-model OCR now makes ratecon parsing nearly free, where it would have needed a data-entry team three years ago.
revenue_model: Shipper SaaS at $1.5k to $6k a month, or 10 to 15% of first-year savings after a re-bid. Owner-operators freemium, with $19 a month for lane-level broker-take data. Anonymized benchmark reports to procurement consultancies and private-equity operating partners.
non_obvious_insight: The freight-audit industry is blind to carrier payout because it is the broker's proprietary secret. Only drivers hold the other half, as ratecon photos on their phones. Individual carriers who invoke 371.3 get ghosted, but a shipper with contractual audit rights gets an answer, and shippers are the ones who can pay. Drivers are free supply, shippers are paying demand, and neither can build this alone. Handle rate-confirmation confidentiality clauses by publishing only anonymized aggregates and letting shippers request records under their own audit rights.
first_30_days: Build a ratecon email and SMS intake bot in about a week. Seed it with 100 owner-operators from OOIDA-style Facebook groups by offering a free 'your rate vs. lane average' check. Collect 2,000 ratecons in the first month. Through freight consultants and PE operating partners, offer 10 mid-size shippers a free one-lane spread report built from their last 12 months of invoices plus the crowd data. Convert the first 2 to 3 to a $2k a month pilot.

title: Tariff Refund Claim Files for Small Importers
one_liner: Turn a small importer's messy customs data into a refund-ready, financeable claim ledger, paid by success fee or on sale of the claim.
customer: US importers of record with roughly $50K to $5M of IEEPA duties who lack in-house customs staff, plus the licensed customs brokers serving them. Claim-buying funds and lenders are the second payer, paying a per-file diligence fee.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026 and the CIT ordered refunds. CBP's CAPE tool has accepted about $134.7B of the roughly $166B pool as of September 11, 2026. The tail sits with the smallest importers. Their ACE accounts are unapproved, they missed the 90-day request window, or their entries are liquidated beyond the 80-day reprocessing window, which the DOJ is appealing at the Federal Circuit. Phase 3, for liquidated entries, was slated for October 6 but delayed. Many are selling claims at deep discounts out of fear or confusion.
solution: Ingest ACE entry-summary reports, broker CSVs and payment records. Map every line to the IEEPA HTS 9903 lines. Compute per-entry phase eligibility, liquidation dates and protest deadlines. Flag duplicate or wrong importer-of-record entries, drawback and FTZ overlaps, and interest owed. Output CAPE-ready batches plus a chain-of-title 'claim data room' with a probability-weighted value for the appeal-dependent entries. A licensed broker partner files, so the product stays software plus workflow. The same engine reprocesses future tariff refunds and exclusions.
why_now: The window is open now: CAPE phases run through fall 2026, the Federal Circuit appeal will set the value of the liquidated tail, and hedge funds and lenders are already buying refund claims. Successor tariffs under other statutes create the same entry-level data problem next year.
revenue_model: 8 to 12% success fee on refunds recovered. A 2 to 4% origination fee when a claim is sold or financed. $500 to $2,000 per-claim diligence files sold to buyers. A subscription for customs brokers who use it across their book.
non_obvious_insight: Distressed-claims desks (Lehman, FTX, Celsius trade claims) know a claim's price is set less by the underlying merits than by documentation quality, chain of title and timing. Whoever standardizes the data room becomes the market's gatekeeper. The small-importer tail is mispriced because sellers can't prove what they are owed, and buyers can't underwrite what they can't verify. The moat is the underwriting file, not the filing.
first_30_days: Build an ES-003 and ACE CSV parser with two or three friendly licensed customs brokers. Offer a free 'refund gap audit' to 30 small importers found through public importer lists. Sign 10 on contingency. Get letters of intent from one or two claim buyers wanting standardized diligence files.

title: Tariff Refund Recovery for Dead Importers
one_liner: A contingency service that finds failed or dormant importers whose IEEPA refund claims are stranded, revives them or works through their bankruptcy trustee, and files the claims through a licensed broker.
customer: Chapter 7 trustees and ABC assignees of failed importers, plus founders of dissolved or dormant small importers. They pay 20-30% of recovered dollars. Secondary customers are claim buyers who want vetted entry-level claim files.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP is now refunding through CAPE in phases: Phase 1 opened Apr 20 for unliquidated and recently liquidated entries, Phase 2 came in June, and Phase 3 (late July) covers finally liquidated entries only for importers who sued at the CIT. Refunds go to the importer of record (or the broker who filed the entry). Every entry has its own clock, including the 180-day protest window. A large tail of small importers closed or went dark during the 2025 tariff shock. Their refunds are six-figure receivables spread across hundreds of ACE entries. They appear on nobody's balance sheet, and nobody at the dead company is watching for them. A trustee liquidating the estate usually does not know the asset exists.
solution: Build an entry-level refund estimator from public bill-of-lading data, HTS lines, country of origin and the IEEPA rate schedule. Cross-match importer names against state dissolution lists and PACER filings to rank stranded claims by likely dollar value. Then run the recovery: (1) approach trustees with an asset-discovery letter and a court-approvable contingency engagement; (2) for dissolved entities, reinstate the corporation under state law, re-enroll ACH, and file CF-4811 designations where needed; (3) have a licensed broker file CAPE declarations for the entries that broker filed; (4) send finally liquidated entries to partner trade counsel for CIT reliquidation orders under the July 17 order. The moat is a licensed-broker partner plus a pipeline of claims that nobody else is hunting.
why_now: IEEPA was struck down Feb 20, 2026. CAPE phases rolled out Apr-Jul 2026, and the July 17 CIT order created a court-driven Phase 3. Per-entry deadlines are now running. Existing refund tools (deadline trackers and CAPE filing helpers) all sell to living importers who are already paying attention. Nobody productized the orphaned-claim hunt.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on refunds recovered, plus interest. Trustee engagements are approved by the bankruptcy court as contingency fee arrangements. A secondary line sells diligenced claim packages to claim buyers at a flat fee per package.
non_obvious_insight: The refund is attached to the importer-of-record number, not to whoever was actually hurt, and only the IOR or the filing broker can claim it in the early phases. Brokers hold the entry data but their powers of attorney die with the client, and chasing a dead client is unbillable work, so nobody does it. A broker can still file CAPE for entries it filed, which makes the broker the key that unlocks these claims. Outsiders see the refund as a tax-accounting topic. Insiders see it as an unclaimed-property hunt across ACE.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull 2025 importer-level volumes for China, Vietnam, India and other tariffed origins from ImportYeti or a cheap paid BOL feed, then estimate each importer's IEEPA duty. Week 2: cross-match against CA, NY, TX, FL and NJ dissolution records and PACER chapter 7 and ABC filings, and rank the top 150 targets above about $50k. Week 3: send trustees a one-page asset-discovery letter, since trustee contact info is public, and have a trade lawyer draft the contingency engagement. Week 4: sign the first 3-5 estates, or dormant founders, and file the first CAPE declarations through the partner broker.

title: Trusted Firmware for Chinese-Made Robots
one_liner: A security-audited, network-isolated software and attestation layer that lets US labs, utilities and cities legally buy and run cheap Unitree-class robots.
customer: US universities and research labs, utilities, municipal fleets, critical-infrastructure operators, and integrators reselling Chinese quadrupeds and humanoids.
problem: Chinese makers hold 86% of humanoid shipments and their robots cost a fraction of US alternatives, but security teams block procurement over cloud telemetry, remote access and radio vulnerabilities disclosed in 2025. There is no neutral, certified 'clean' stack, and barriers are going up.
solution: A replacement software stack and wrapper: local-only operation, cloud services removed, wireless interfaces locked down, signed OTA updates under customer keys, an SBOM, and a continuous-audit attestation report that security auditors accept. Add an optional network-quarantine gateway appliance.
why_now: Tariffs, the FCC's DJI action and expected legislation are tightening. Unitree's IPO signals the supply will keep coming, so buyers with budgets are stuck between the price advantage and compliance.
revenue_model: $500-1,500 per robot a year for the license and updates, $10-30k per security assessment, and about $800 per gateway appliance.
non_obvious_insight: Each time the US restricts a Chinese hardware category, a trust layer becomes the only route for legal buyers. Everyone bets on which hardware wins, but the money sits in the compliance gap. Risk: an outright ban would kill the market, so design for a pivot to open-source or allied hardware.
first_30_days: Buy a Go2 and a G1, reproduce the publicly documented vulnerabilities, and publish a hardening guide. Offer free audits to 5 university robotics labs' IT security officers and convert 3 to paid assessments at $10-15k.

title: Closed-School Science Labs Shipped to African Schools
angle: Education, credentialing and skills after AI x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: Take decommissioned lab benches, microscopes, fume hoods and Chromebooks from US schools being closed, refurbish them into container-sized lab packages with a practical-exam curriculum, and sell them to private secondary schools in East and West Africa.
customer: Buyers are private and faith-based secondary school networks in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria and Ghana, paying $8-15k per lab package. Sellers are US districts, charters and private schools that are closing and want fast, lawful disposal at low cost.
problem: More than 1,000 US public schools closed in 2025-26. Chicago alone has 135k empty seats, and Portland, Minneapolis and Albuquerque are queued behind it. Districts dispose of equipment through slow public-surplus auctions that recover pennies. Meanwhile African private schools running on tiny per-student budgets cannot afford lab equipment, even though national practical exams and newer competency-based curricula require it. A new lab costs $30-50k and takes months to import.
solution: Inventory soon-to-close buildings and remove complete science rooms, robotics kits, libraries and tested Chromebooks (with NIST-grade data wipes and export of working goods only). Bundle them into a 40-foot container with local installation, a practical-exam curriculum (matched to Kenyan, Nigerian or Ghanaian exam boards), a one-day teacher orientation, and a small annual refill of consumables. The district gets a disposal certificate and a possible donation receipt.
why_now: Closures are at a four-year high, so supply is predictable and geographically concentrated. The AI memory crunch, with memory now 30-40% of a device's bill of materials, has raised new-device prices and made used Chromebooks valuable. Distributed solar and batteries mean African schools can now run lab equipment and computers. As I understand it, Kenya's first competency-based senior-school cohort (2026) requires STEM practicals many schools cannot deliver.
revenue_model: Lab packages sell at $9-14k against a landed cost of $5-6k. A curriculum and refill subscription adds $600 per school per year. Districts pay a $1-3k decommissioning fee per closure in place of an auction consignment fee, or grant surplus title for free.
non_obvious_insight: A closing school is a fully assembled, curriculum-matched capital asset that public procurement can only sell by the pound, while the same asset is the binding constraint on practical-exam pass rates in low-fee African schools. The margin is in the bundle of equipment, practical curriculum and teacher orientation, not in the equipment, and that bundle is exactly what charity donation programs do not offer.
first_30_days: Pick one district and walk three soon-to-close buildings. Offer free removal of the first 10 science rooms in exchange for title to the equipment. Get letters of intent and 30% deposits from two or three African private-school owners through diaspora, church or school-association networks. Ship one container of two labs plus 200 tested Chromebooks. Line up an export broker and a data-wipe vendor before touching anything.

title: Pallet Co-Op for Micro-Resellers
one_liner: A distributor for one-person resellers that buys store-closing truckloads, values them SKU by SKU, and splits them into size-matched $150 to $500 shares delivered to each member.
customer: Under-25 and hobbyist resellers (roughly 3 to 100 sales per week) who currently buy at retail or from other resellers. They pay a markup of 8% to 15% plus a $19 per month membership.
problem: Real wholesale margins are locked behind minimum order quantities and size-run mismatch. A liquidator lot has 240 pairs, but 60% are size 6 or size 13 that nobody wants to hold. Mystery pallets are priced as a percentage of MSRP, not by what a SKU actually resells for, so buyers overpay for junk and underbid the winners. Discord 'group buys' exist but run on trust and screenshots, and they collapse when someone ghosts on payment.
solution: We buy truckload and pallet lots from liquidators and closing retailers, run the manifest against resale comps to price every line, and slice it: each member gets a share of the SKUs and sizes they selected, with the top-value pairs allocated by lottery so nobody feels cheated. Deposits are collected before we buy, so we carry almost no inventory risk. A partnered 3PL or a garage-and-labels crew ships each member's slice within a week. Later: net-14 financing on shares and buy-back of unsold slow-moving sizes.
why_now: Retail contraction is producing a steady stream of liquidation lots in 2025-26: Foot Locker is being folded into Dick's with store consolidation, other mall and footwear chains are closing doors, and brands reset inventory after tariff and demand swings. Margins on hyped Nike pairs are thin, so only good buying keeps micro-resellers alive. Cheap vision models make manifest-to-comp valuation nearly free.
revenue_model: 8% to 15% markup on each share plus $19 per month membership. Later, interest on short-term inventory financing and fees for a 'sell-through insurance' tier.
non_obvious_insight: Capital is not what stops small resellers from wholesale. Break-bulk is. Nobody sells a truckload in 40 slices sorted by size. The person who does the boring sorting, allocating and shipping becomes the small reseller's Costco. Because valuation uses resale comps rather than MSRP percent, the co-op can quietly outbid mystery-pallet buyers on the best lots.
first_30_days: Find one liquidator willing to sell a 5 to 10 pallet lot of mixed sneakers and apparel. Pre-sell 40 slots at $250 each in a Discord with deposits before buying anything, using the manifest value as the pitch. Rent a garage or use a local prep center. Ship in 10 days, collect testimonials and reviews, then run the next lot every week.

title: Cross-Border Income Passport for Freelancers
one_liner: Give stablecoin-paid remote workers a verifiable, portable income record that landlords, lenders and visa agents accept.
customer: Freelancers and remote workers in Nigeria, the Philippines, Colombia and Kenya; landlords, lenders and visa agents pay to verify.
problem: Freelancers cannot get portable income records for loans or visas, and stablecoin and platform-wallet earnings leave no bank paper trail.
solution: Connect wallets, payout platforms and invoices, then produce signed income attestations with a QR verification link. The wedge is rental and visa income letters at about $15 each for remote workers in Lagos and Manila.
why_now: Stablecoin payroll and invoicing tools like Bloccpay are spreading, Flutterwave and Yellow Card are scaling, and LatAm lenders are hunting for new borrowers.
revenue_model: $10-20 per attestation, plus $1-3 per verification call from lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in stablecoin income is proving it, not moving it. Whoever gets accepted by three lenders becomes a bureau for the remote-work diaspora.
first_30_days: Build attestations from Payoneer, Wise and USDC statements and test with 50 workers and one landlord network.

title: GLP-1 Off-Ramp Program for Cash-Pay Prescribers
one_liner: A structured 12-week landing program for people stopping GLP-1 drugs, sold to the prescribers who lose revenue the day a patient quits.
customer: Independent obesity-medicine clinics, med spas and cash-pay telehealth prescribers (pay per enrollee); secondary: patients paying $149-249 for the program.
problem: Every fitness and nutrition company is building for people ON the drug. But real-world data suggest up to roughly 65 percent quit within a year, and a 2026 meta-regression finds about 60 percent of lost weight returns within a year of stopping (individual studies vary). The discontinuation moment is unowned: prescribers lose the patient, gyms never see them, and regain triggers shame and churn.
solution: A program keyed to the last-dose date: taper coordination with the prescriber, protein and resistance-training progression, weekly connected-scale weigh-ins, human coach check-ins on hunger and food noise, and pre-agreed re-start triggers (for example +3 percent regain) that route the patient back to the prescriber. Delivered by app plus partner gyms.
why_now: Oral GLP-1s at $149-299 cash (Wegovy pill launched Dec 2025/Jan 2026, orforglipron in April 2026) make starting cheap and stopping easy; about 1 in 8 US adults report currently taking one; cash-pay churn is the biggest leak in prescriber P&Ls.
revenue_model: $150-300 per enrollee paid by the prescriber as a retention and win-back tool (or $199 patient-paid), plus a revenue share on patients who restart therapy.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the prescriber, not the patient: the off-ramp is a retention product for the clinic's P&L, and a regain alert doubles as a win-back lead. Evidence on who regains is mixed, so a regain-risk model built from your own cohort becomes the proprietary asset.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 independent clinics or med spas, enroll 30 patients ending therapy using an off-the-shelf connected scale, messaging tool and a lifting template, and track 90-day weight, lean-mass proxy and restart rate versus each clinic's history to use as the sales proof.

title: Sensor-Priced Insurance for Recovery and Peptide Clinics
angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
one_liner: A specialty insurance program that covers contrast-therapy studios, IV and peptide bars and sauna clubs at lower premiums when their sauna, cold-plunge and session logs are streamed as underwriting data.
customer: Independent and small-franchise recovery studios and med-spa or peptide clinics with 1-5 locations, paying $4-12k a year per location. Excess-and-surplus carriers and wholesalers are the capacity partners.
problem: Standard general-liability policies exclude or misclassify saunas, cold plunges, IV therapy and peptides. Carriers have no loss history, so operators buy expensive surplus-lines cover. The real exposures are burns, syncope, slip-and-fall, water-quality infections such as Legionella, and unlicensed practice. Franchise growth in recovery is outrunning the insurance market.
solution: Start as a program manager or agency and grow into an MGA with a fronting carrier and reinsurance. Studios install a roughly $60-250 sensor kit that logs plunge temperature and sanitizer levels, sauna temperature and duration, session counts, waiver and health-screen completion, and staff certifications. A sensor-verified studio earns up to a 25% credit. The program adds an incident-reporting protocol, risk-engineering checklists and, over time, a proprietary claims pool.
why_now: HHS moved most Category 2 peptides back toward compoundable status in Feb 2026, and an FDA panel backed BPC-157 and KPV on July 23, 2026, so peptides are entering clinics and recovery bars without a malpractice rating. Reinsurance is softening, with Jefferies expecting declines through 2027, and record cat-bond and traditional capital means niche programs can find cheap capacity. Recovery studios are among the fastest-growing small-format wellness businesses.
revenue_model: Commission of 12-15%, an MGA fee of 5-8% of premium, and a profit commission. Sensors and software add $49 a month. 500 locations at $8k premium is $4M of premium and about $700k of revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Underwriters have no loss data on cold plunges and the operators are the only ones who can generate it. A sensor-verified studio is a better risk than a paper-verified one, so the data flywheel is the moat. This is one of the first classes where the insured object, a plunge tank or sauna, can report its own hygiene and temperature.
first_30_days: Partner with a retail broker or E&S wholesaler that has a fitness or spa book. Get indicative terms from two E&S carriers on a credit for sensor-verified operators. Recruit 10 design-partner studios through owner communities and sauna or plunge dealer lists, giving them free sensor kits in exchange for logs. Aim for firm quotes within 90 days, and confirm licensing needs with counsel before quoting anything.
